issues.legal_issue: Relatives’ litigation does not extend relief to a non-party unless they represented that person expressly or by necessary implication.
material_facts: A father and brother had brought an earlier writ petition in their own right, and the later claimant was not a party to it.
Neither relative stated or implied that they were acting for the later claimant.
The earlier proceedings did not plead a coparcenary with the later claimant, and the appellate order confined relief to the relatives’ land.
issues.conclusion: The earlier litigation did not include the later claimant or extend its relief to him.
issues.legal_principle: In A. Viswanatha Pillai v. Special Tahsildar for Land Acquisition No. IV, a co-owner’s reference application was treated as having been made for other co-owners because it expressly or by necessary implication sought a reference on their behalf. That reasoning did not apply here because no such representation was made in the earlier litigation.

rule.if: later_writ_relies_on_relative_case and not claimant_named_in_prior_case and not relatives_asserted_representation

predicates.later_writ_relies_on_relative_case: A claimant brings a later writ proceeding relying on litigation previously brought by relatives.
predicates.claimant_named_in_prior_case: The claimant was named as a party in the relatives’ earlier proceeding.
predicates.relatives_asserted_representation: The relatives stated expressly or by necessary implication that they were acting on the claimant’s behalf.

issues.definition: When a later writ relies on relatives’ litigation, relief from that litigation does not extend to a claimant who was not a party if the relatives did not represent that claimant.

issues.legal_issue: Brothers cannot claim a coparcenary between themselves by excluding their father when the father is present.
material_facts: The claimant asserted co-ownership or coparcenary with his brother alone.
The claimant did not plead a coparcenary with his father and brother together.
issues.conclusion: There could be no coparcenary between the brothers alone by excluding their father in the father’s presence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the stated Hindu-law principle that, in the presence of a father, a coparcenary cannot exist between brothers alone by excluding the father.

predicates.coparcenary_claimed_between_brothers_onl: A claimant asserts a coparcenary with a brother while excluding their father.
predicates.father_present: The father is present in the family circumstances relevant to the asserted coparcenary.

issues.definition: A claim of coparcenary between brothers alone is not recognized when their father is present and excluded from the claim.

issues.legal_issue: One co-owner’s response to a land acquisition does not by itself determine another co-owner’s right to challenge the acquisition or seek compensation.
material_facts: The claimant and his brother asserted interests in land subject to acquisition.
The claimant accepted compensation under protest and sought enhancement, while his brother had challenged the acquisition.
The Court considered that co-owners may make different choices about challenging an acquisition and seeking compensation.
issues.conclusion: A co-owner’s acceptance of compensation does not estop another co-owner from challenging the acquisition, and one co-owner’s challenge does not affect another co-owner merely because that person accepted the acquisition and compensation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated co-owners’ rights in acquisition proceedings as independent: one may challenge the acquisition while another accepts compensation or seeks its enhancement. It distinguished A. Viswanatha Pillai, which concerned whether a reference application by one co-owner had been made on behalf of the others.

rule.if: land_acquisition_dispute and co_ownership and (another_coowner_accepted_compensation or another_coowner_challenged_acquisition)

predicates.land_acquisition_dispute: The dispute concerns the acquisition of land.
predicates.co_ownership: More than one person has an ownership interest in the land.
predicates.another_coowner_accepted_compensation: A co-owner accepted compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.another_coowner_challenged_acquisition: A co-owner challenged the acquisition of the land.

issues.definition: In a land acquisition dispute involving co-owners, one co-owner’s acceptance of compensation or challenge to the acquisition does not by itself determine the other co-owners’ rights.

issues.legal_issue: Accepting compensation under protest preserves the ability to seek a reference on award matters but does not, by itself, show that the claimant preserved a challenge to the acquisition.
material_facts: The claimant accepted the Collector’s compensation under protest and applied for enhancement before the competent court.
The claimant’s writ petition challenging the acquisition was filed after the award and approximately five years after the notification.
The Court found that the protest was made to preserve the right to seek a reference on matters covered by the award, not to safeguard a challenge to the acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The claimant’s acceptance of compensation under protest protected the remedy of reference concerning award matters; it did not establish that he had preserved a challenge to the acquisition itself.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, allows an interested person to seek a reference only if that person has not accepted the award. Acceptance of compensation under protest indicates non-acceptance for that purpose, because acceptance without protest may result in loss of the right to a reference on matters covered by Section 18.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_dispute: The proceeding concerns compensation awarded for acquired land.
predicates.compensation_accepted_under_protest: The claimant accepted the awarded compensation while expressly maintaining a protest.
predicates.claimant_seeks_reference_on_award_matter: The claimant seeks a reference for determination of matters relating to the award.

issues.definition: When a claimant accepts compensation under protest and seeks determination of award matters, the reference remedy is preserved for those matters.

issues.legal_issue: A factual plea not raised before the High Court cannot be introduced for the first time in an appeal when the High Court’s recorded order states the contention made there.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the dismissal of a writ petition concerning land acquisition.
The High Court’s order recorded the contention that the earlier appellate decision was wrong and stated that no other point was urged.
Before the Supreme Court, the claimant said that a different contention had been made before the High Court, but the Court found that the recorded order reflected the submissions made in open court.
The claimant had not sought correction from the High Court if he disputed its record of the arguments.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not raise the new plea in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a plea about what was argued before the High Court could not be permitted for the first time in the appeal when the High Court’s order recorded the arguments and the claimant had not approached that court with a grievance about its record.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: A party appeals from the dismissal of a writ petition.
predicates.new_factual_plea_not_raised_below: The party advances a factual contention in the appeal that was not raised before the High Court.
predicates.high_court_order_records_arguments: The High Court’s order records the arguments made before it.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a dismissed writ petition, a new factual plea is not entertained when it was not raised below and the High Court’s order records the arguments made.
